                                            Direct Testimony

                                                on behalf of


                                   Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company

        Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey                                 Page 1 of 29

    1   Q.     Please state your name and business address.
    2   A.     My name is Matthew DeCourcey. My business address is 200 Clarendon Street, Boston,
    3          MA 02116.
    4
    5   Q.     By whom are you employed and in what capacity?
    6   A.     I am employed by Charles River Associates (“CRA”) as a Vice President in the Energy
    7          Practice.
    8
    9   Q.     On whose behalf are you testifying?
   10   A.     I am providing this testimony on behalf of Oklahoma Gas & Electric Company (“OG&E”
   11          or the “Company”).
   12
   13   Q.     Please summarize your educational background and professional qualifications.
   14   A.     I have spent more than twenty years working in the regulated energy space, including
   15          consulting and in-house utility roles. In my current role at CRA, I advise utilities, investors,
   16          policymakers, and institutional consumers on a wide range of matters related to utility
   17          regulation and finance, including regulatory strategy, due diligence for regulated assets,
   18          market analysis, and investment strategy, among others.              In addition, my clients
   19          periodically ask me to represent them in rate cases and similar proceedings before state,
   20          federal, and provincial regulators.
   21                 Prior to joining CRA in 2025, I led the regulatory department at Liberty Utilities
   22          (“Liberty”) as Vice President for Rates and Regulatory Strategy where I was responsible
   23          for all matters pertaining to ratemaking and regulatory engagement for all of Liberty’s
   24          operating companies, which included electric, gas, and water utilities doing business in
   25          thirteen U.S. states, Canada, Bermuda, and Chile.          Included among those operating
   26          companies is the Empire District Electric Company (“Empire District”), which serves
   27          around 5,000 retail customers in Oklahoma.
   28                  Before joining Liberty, I held increasingly senior roles with several consultancies
   29          providing energy services to the energy industry. Most recently among those, I was a
   30          Managing Director in the Power & Utilities Practice at FTI Consulting.



        Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey                                            Page 2 of 29
        Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 4 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 30




    1                  I received my undergraduate degree in Political Science from the University of
    2          Massachusetts at Boston and my Master of Business Administration from the University
    3          of Massachusetts at Amherst.
    4
    5   Q.     Can you please describe the extent of your professional experience in matters related
    6          to the regulation of electric service to large load customers?
    7   A.     Since joining CRA, ratemaking and regulation pertaining to large load customers (data
    8          centers) has been a primary focus of my practice. During that time, I have advised multiple
    9          “hyperscalers” on regulatory and commercial strategies related to grid interconnection and
   10          energy supply. I have advised U.S. utilities on similar topics that include, among other
   11          things, ratemaking for data centers; infrastructure financing; and analyses of current and
   12          future impacts of data centers on the electric grid, on the industry, and on customers. I
   13          have also been retained by investors, policy makers, and other market participants to lend
   14          my insight on these topics and support their planning and decision-making.
   15                  I have also participated in thought leadership on the subject of the regulation of data
   16          centers. On several occasions I have been invited to present on matters related to load
   17          growth and data centers at significant industry events. I have been interviewed by industry
   18          publications and general interest media on topics related to data centers and utility rates
   19          and I have authored or co-authored multiple publications. Most recently, I was one of the
   20          authors of a major report commissioned by the Edison Electric Institute examining recent
   21          trends in retail electric rates and affordability that devoted significant focus to the question
   22          of data centers’ impacts on existing customers and the protections for them that utilities
   23          and regulators are embedding in the transactions and ratemaking.
   24                  During this time, CRA has emerged as a leading expert on data centers and load
   25          growth, offering a wide range of insight and expertise beyond my areas of specialization
   26          that include load forecasting, resource adequacy and system planning, interconnection
   27          issues, market design, and related matters.




        Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey                                            Page 3 of 29
        Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 4 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 30




    1   Q.     Have you testified previously before the Oklahoma Corporation Commission (the
    2          “Commission”) or before any other utility regulator?
    3   A.     Yes. I recently filed testimony on OG&E’s behalf in Case No. PUD2026-000031, where
    4          I addressed the protections for customers put into place in Energy Service Agreements
    5          (“ESAs”) between the Company and a subsidiary of Google Energy, LLC (the “Google
    6          ESAs”). Prior to that, I appeared before the Commission in Case No. PUD2021-000163
    7          on behalf of Empire District. I have also made appearances before utility regulators in
    8          other jurisdictions. A current copy of my resume is provided as Exhibit MD-1 and provides
    9          additional details.
   10
   11   Q.     What is the purpose of your testimony?
   12   A.     My testimony supports the Company’s proposed Extra Large Power and Light Tariff
   13          (“XLPL Tariff” or the “Tariff”). Specifically, my testimony describes the ways in which
   14          the Tariff will protect OG&E’s customers against the risk of stranded costs and cross
   15          subsidization of costs across rate classes. I also explain why adding XLPL customers could
   16          reduce rates for the Company’s existing customers.
   17
   18   Q.     Please describe the documents you reviewed.
   19   A.     In addition to the documents and datasets that are cited in my testimony, I reviewed a copy
   20          of the draft XLPL Tariff, which was provided to me by OG&E.
   21
   22   Q.     Did your review also include documents that are separate from the XLPL Tariff, but
   23          which are incorporated by reference?
   24   A.     Yes, in addition to the tariff itself, I reviewed the Terms and Conditions of Service for
   25          Extra Large Load Customers (“T&CXLLC”) applicable to customers taking service under
   26          the XLPL Tariff. Embedded within the T&CXLLC is the Preliminary Agreement (“PA”),
   27          which appears at Section 513 of the T&CXLLC and which defines the contractual
   28          relationship between OG&E and a large load customer during the period prior to which the
   29          Company first delivers electricity, and the Electric Service Agreement (“ESA”), which
   30          appears at Section 514 and defines contract terms once service begins. For the remainder
   31          of my testimony, references to the XLPL Tariff should be assumed to incorporate the

        Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey                                        Page 4 of 29
        Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 4 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 30




    1          T&CXLLC, the PA, and the ESA unless otherwise noted. The only distinction I make
    2          between them is for the purpose of referencing citations.
    3
    4   Q.     After your review, what have you concluded about the XLPL Tariff?
    5   A.     That it provides OG&E’s customers with robust protections against adverse outcomes.
    6          Specifically, I conclude the following:
    7                 First, there is general recognition across the industry that utilities seeking
    8          authorization to serve new large load customers must demonstrate that existing customers
    9          are protected from the potential adverse effects of stranded costs and that existing
   10          customers will not subsidize the cost to serve the large loads. Where that has been the case,
   11          regulators have generally approved large load tariffs and special contracts.
   12                 Second, the terms of the XLPL Tariff will help protect OG&E’s existing customers
   13          from stranded costs and from any subsidization of the costs of large load entrants.
   14                 Third, adding XLPL customers to the OG&E system could reduce rates for existing
   15          customers.
   16                 On the basis of these conclusions, I recommend that the Commission approve the
   17          XLPL Tariff without modification.
   18
   19   Q.     How is the remainder of your testimony organized?
   20   A.     In Section I, I define stranded costs and cross-subsidies among rate classes and explain that
   21          protecting customers from risks associated with those two outcomes is a primary
   22          consideration when designing the tariffs and rates that govern service to new large load
   23          customers. In Section II and Section III, I describe the ways in which the XLPL Tariff will
   24          protect customers against risks associated with stranded costs and cross-subsidies,
   25          respectively. Section IV describes why utility rates for OG&E’s existing customers are
   26          likely to be lower if XLPL customers are added to the system.




        Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey                                          Page 5 of 29
        Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 4 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 30




    1    I.    CUSTOMER PROTECTIONS FOCUS ON AVOIDING STRANDED COSTS AND
    2                              CROSS-SUBSIDIES AMONG CLASSES


    3   Q.     Please explain the concept of stranded assets.
    4   A.     Stranded assets are assets that a utility has invested in but which it cannot recover in the
    5          normal course of business. In the context of large load ratemaking, stranded assets would
    6          most likely be caused if a utility made investments to serve a new, large load customer but
    7          the customer subsequently left the system before the costs of those investments could be
    8          recovered. Stranded assets can impact existing customers if the utility is required to
    9          recover the costs of its investment from them.
   10
   11   Q.     Please explain the concept of cross-subsidies among rate classes.
   12   A.     A cross-subsidy occurs when the rates a given customer class pays for the utility’s cost of
   13          providing service to that class also contribute to paying for the costs of serving another
   14          customer class. In the context of this proceeding, it is important that OG&E’s existing
   15          customers do not subsidize the cost of serving XLPL customers.
   16
   17   Q.     Has the Public Utilities Division (“PUD”) commented on stranded costs and cross-
   18          subsidies?
   19   A.     Yes, it has. In a June 2025 memorandum to the Commission, PUD identifies the risks that
   20          it believes should be the primary focus of regulatory review in proceedings regarding
   21          service to data centers. The memorandum’s conclusions are consistent with mine in that it
   22          identifies the avoidance of stranded costs and cross-subsidies as among the small handful
   23          of “key regulatory issues” that will need to be resolved to successfully integrate data center
   24          loads onto the grid. 1




        1
               The other “key regulatory issues” identified in the PUD memorandum relate to system planning
               and resource adequacy, each of which are addressed by other witnesses testifying on behalf of the
               Company. Oklahoma Corporation Commission, Public Utility Division Memorandum on Large
               Load Research, June 3, 2025, https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/occ/documents/ajls/jls-
               courts/court-clerk/meetings/meeting-presentations-
               2025/PUD%20Large%20Load%20Research%206-3-25.pdf.


        Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey                                             Page 6 of 29
        Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 4 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 30




    1   Q.     Have regulators in other jurisdictions also focused on these risks as a primary
    2          consideration?
    3   A.     Consistently.    Generally speaking, regulators are very interested in the benefits to
    4          ratepayers that could accrue from adding large loads, but only if the risks of stranded costs
    5          and cost subsidies can be mitigated. For example, in my testimony supporting the Google
    6          ESAs (Case No. PUD2026-000031), I discussed a recent decision by the Michigan Public
    7          Service Commission (“MPSC”) to approve new tariffs for service to large load customers
    8          in Consumers Energy’s service territory. In a press release that was issued at the same time
    9          as its decision, the MPSC explained the key considerations at hand in the proceeding:
   10                   The Commission said its aim in the proceeding was to harness potential
   11                   benefits to the electric grid while ensuring that these new large load
   12                   customers fully pay for the costs needed to serve them, and that there are
   13                   adequate guardrails in place to avoid both cross-subsidization from other
   14                   customers and the risk of stranded costs that would be paid by other
   15                   customers should the anticipated load fail to fully materialize. 2

   16          In my experience, the MPSC’s interest in the potential benefits that could come with adding
   17          large load customers to the grid and the need to address risks associated with stranded cost
   18          and cross-subsidization are both typical. These issues have been carefully considered in
   19          every ratemaking proceeding related to utility service for new data centers of which I am
   20          aware.
   21
   22   Q.     Do you think these are the issues that the Commission should consider in this
   23          proceeding?
   24   A.     Yes, I do. If the Commission concludes that the provisions of the XLPL Tariff protect
   25          OG&E’s customers from the risk of stranded costs and that existing customers will not
   26          subsidize the cost of serving new large load customers on the XLPL Tariff, then I believe
   27          it should approve the tariff. In the sections that follow, I explain why I believe this to be
   28          the case.



        2
               Michigan Public Service Commission, MPSC approves terms of service between Consumers
               Energy and data centers, other large other very large customers; adds protections for existing
               customers, November 6, 2026, https://mi-
               psc.my.site.com/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/068cs00001ORFPlAAP.

    1        II. THE XLPL TARIFF PROTECTS OG&E’S CUSTOMERS FROM STRANDED
    2                                                COSTS


    3   Q.     Why are stranded costs a particular concern in the context of service to large loads?
    4   A.     Because the investments required to serve large loads can be very large and because those
    5          investments are often made to develop infrastructure that serves a single customer. As a
    6          result, a utility could incur significant stranded costs because of unexpected events that
    7          impact a single business or customer.
    8
    9   Q.     How can stranded cost risk be mitigated?
   10   A.     Utilities try to mitigate the risk by imposing terms of service that require a new large load
   11          customer to make a financial commitment to fulfilling its contractual obligations.
   12
   13   Q.     How is that achieved?
   14   A.     By imposing terms of service that include the following obligations: (1) the requirement
   15          that new customers fund transmission and distribution (“T&D”) infrastructure costs that
   16          would be incurred to provide service, (2) execution of a long-term, binding contract for
   17          service, (3) inclusion of significant bill minimums that ensure payments from the customer
   18          that are close to contracted amounts even if the customer uses less energy than expected,
   19          (4), limitations on contract termination and the imposition of significant fees upon
   20          customers who terminate service or reduce their capacity needs, and (5) creditworthiness
   21          requirements that require the provision of a financial assurance, sometimes called
   22          collateral.
   23
   24   Q.     Are these terms in widespread use in the energy industry?
   25   A.     Yes, most utilities serving data center customers will have some, most, or all of these
   26          protections in place as a condition of providing service.
   27
   28   Q.     Are all of these mechanisms included in the XLPL Tariff?
   29   A.     Yes.



        Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey                                          Page 8 of 29
        Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 4 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 9 OF 30




    1   Q.     Please explain how the XLPL Tariff imposes the first obligation, that large load
    2          customers fund the T&D costs of providing utility service.
    3   A.     Section 505 of the T&CXLLC requires that customers taking service under the tariff are
    4          required to fund 100% of the T&D infrastructure costs associated with serving their new
    5          or expanded load through a Contribution in Aid of Construction (“CIAC”). Section 3 of
    6          the PA (T&CXLLC Section 513) requires the customer to make full payment of the
    7          estimated costs before construction can begin. In addition, Section 5.01 of the ESA
    8          indicates that if OG&E determines later that T&D investments are required later, the
    9          customer will also fund those investments via a CIAC.
   10
   11   Q.     How much does the requirement to fund infrastructure via CIAC payments help to
   12          mitigate the risk of stranded costs?
   13   A.     Requiring new customers to pay for the T&D infrastructure that will be developed to serve
   14          them completely eliminates the risk of stranded costs associated with those investments.
   15
   16   Q.     How does this provision eliminate this risk?
   17   A.     Because OG&E will receive 100 percent of the costs for T&D investments that could
   18          otherwise become stranded if the XLPL customer’s load does not materialize, there are no
   19          costs that could become stranded. In the event an XLPL customer suddenly stopped taking
   20          service or failed to initiate service, there would be no impact to OG&E or its customers
   21          because the costs of the applicable infrastructure would already have been paid by the
   22          customer.
   23
   24   Q.     The second obligation imposed by the XLPL Tariff, which you contend helps to
   25          mitigate stranded cost, is the obligation to commit to a lengthy service term. Please
   26          explain.
   27   A.     Customers taking service under the XLPL Tariff must commit to an Initial Term of service
   28          of fifteen years, which does not begin until the conclusion of a Load Ramp Period that may




        Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey                                       Page 9 of 29
        Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 4 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 10 OF 30




    1          be as long as five years. 3 The Tariff provides opportunities to extend the agreement beyond
    2          the Initial Term.
    3
    4   Q.     Is the service term commitment required by the XLPL Tariff comparable to the
    5          commitment required by other large load tariffs of which you are aware?
    6   A.     The term required in the XLPL Tariff is longer than is required by most large load tariffs
    7          of which I am aware. Later in this section of my testimony I compare the provisions in the
    8          XLPL Tariff to the required term lengths from other large-load tariffs which I reviewed.
    9
   10   Q.     Does the length of the service term commitment influence the degree to which
   11          stranded cost risk is mitigated?
   12   A.     Yes. Longer service term commitments mean less risk of stranded costs, all else equal.
   13
   14   Q.     Is that to say that because the XLPL Tariff requires a longer service term
   15          commitment than do most other large load tariffs that OG&E’s customers are better
   16          protected, all else equal?
   17   A.     Yes.
   18
   19   Q.     Does the fact that all T&D investments will be funded by customer CIAC mean that
   20          stranded cost risk is mitigated, to some degree, regardless of their service term
   21          commitments?
   22   A.     Yes, to some degree. In the context of stranded cost risk, longer terms mean more time for
   23          the utility to recover the cost of investments made on behalf of its customers. Because the
   24          Tariff requires T&D investments to be recovered via CIAC, those costs would not be
   25          stranded at any point in the term of service. That said, the Company and its non-XLPL
   26          customers obviously benefit in other ways from predictable, long-term participation by
   27          large-load customers.




        3
               See Section 504 of the T&CXLLC and Section 1.01 of the ESA.


        Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey                                        Page 10 of 29
        Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 4 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 11 OF 30




    1   Q.     Would you agree that because the XLPL Tariff requires new customers to fund T&D
    2          investments via CIAC and obligates new customers to a comparably longer service
    3          term commitment that it provides a higher level of protection from stranded costs
    4          than do tariffs at other utilities, all else equal?
    5   A.     Yes. Although there are other tariffs for large load service currently in effect that also
    6          provide robust protection against stranded costs, OG&E’s XLPL Tariff imposes
    7          obligations regarding capital investments and service term commitments that are each,
    8          individually, robust. It is reasonable to conclude that the level of protection for OG&E’s
    9          non-XLPL customers is significantly higher than those observed in other utility
   10          jurisdictions, all else equal.
   11
   12   Q.     Minimum billing requirements comprise the third way stranded cost risks are
   13          mitigated. What are the minimums specified in the Tariff?
   14   A.      The Tariff establishes separate minimum billing requirements for demand-based charges
   15          and for energy-based charges.
   16
   17   Q.     Please describe the demand-based minimum charges in the XLPL Tariff.
   18   A.     Each XLPL customer will work with OG&E to establish Billing Contract Demand, which,
   19          as defined in the Tariff, is based on the customer’s load once it has achieved full
   20          commercial operation (e.g., following the Load Ramp Period). Minimum Billing Demand
   21          is a function of Billing Contract Demand. Specifically, the Tariff sets Minimum Billing
   22          Demand at 85 percent of the Billing Contract Demand. Which is to say that regardless of
   23          a customer’s demand during any billing period, it will pay capacity-based charges ($/kW)
   24          as though its demand were at least 85 percent of the amount specified in the Billing
   25          Contract Demand. In periods where its demand is higher, capacity-based charges will be
   26          assessed based on the customer’s actual demand.
   27
   28   Q.     Please describe the energy-based minimum charges in the XLPL Tariff.
   29   A.     The Tariff defines Minimum Billing Energy based on a formula that assumes a 90 percent
   30          load factor, which means that an XLPL customer will pay energy-based charges ($/kWh)
   31          as though it were in operation during 90 percent of the hours in a billing period, even if its

        Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey                                         Page 11 of 29
        Case No. PUD 2026-000046

    1          actual consumption is lower. 4 If consumption is higher, energy-based charges will be paid
    2          based on actual consumption.
    3
    4   Q.     Are these demand and energy billing minimums in the Tariff consistent with those in
    5          place at other utilities of which you are aware?
    6   A.     Most large-load tariffs of which I am aware include some form of minimum billing
    7          requirements; however, the minimums established in the XLPL Tariff are higher than the
    8          minimums set in most of those tariffs. My testimony includes a discussion comparing the
    9          XLPL Tariff with comparable large load utility tariffs, which includes a comparison of
   10          billing minimums.
   11
   12   Q.     You identified exit fees and capacity reduction fees as the fourth mechanism by which
   13          customers are protected from stranded costs. What does the XLPL Tariff require?
   14   A.     The tariff effectively requires a customer to pay at least the minimum charges I described
   15          above for the entirety of the contract term. Put another way, the total payments that an
   16          XLPL customer would make to OG&E would very likely be the same, or very close to the
   17          same, regardless of whether it exercised its rights to terminate its service agreement.
   18
   19   Q.     What makes you say that?
   20   A.     Section 508 of the XLPL Tariff defines the process by which a customer may terminate its
   21          agreement with OG&E or reduce its contract demand. Termination or capacity reduction
   22          is not possible until after the ninth year of the Initial Term (and in the case of capacity
   23          reduction, can only be reduced by 25 percent). Thereafter, an XLPL customer may
   24          terminate the agreement or reduce contract demand upon three years’ notice to OG&E.
   25          During the period in which that notice is pending, the customer will continue to take service
   26          subject to all the Tariff’s provisions, including the required billing minimums. At the end
   27          of the notice period, the customer must pay an Early Termination Exit Fee or the Capacity
   28          Reduction Fee, which will be calculated by the Company, and which could be for the


        4
               The XLPL Tariff provides the formula the Company will use to calculate Minimum Billing
               Energy.


        Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey                                        Page 12 of 29
        Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 4 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 13 OF 30




    1          remaining three years of the minimum billing contract payments. Assuming the three-year
    2          notice period is applied, the XLPL customer would be required to make fifteen years’ worth
    3          of payments.
    4
    5   Q.     Does this structure mitigate stranded cost risk associated with early contract
    6          termination or capacity reductions during the term?
    7   A.     Yes, it does. Every customer taking service under the XLPL Tariff will pay at least the
    8          minimum payments for the ramp-up period and then for the full fifteen years of the Initial
    9          Term.
   10
   11   Q.     Can you please describe how OG&E uses financial assurance to further mitigate
   12          stranded cost risk?
   13   A.     Section 5.04 of the ESA requires XLPL customers to provide financial assurance, or
   14          collateral, in an amount equal to 100% of the minimum charges for five years of minimum
   15          charges at full Billing Contract Demand (e.g., five years’ worth of minimum charges during
   16          the Initial Term).    This requirement reduces the risk of unrecovered costs to other
   17          customers in the event where an XLPL customer does not satisfy its obligations under the
   18          ESA. During the term of service, OG&E will determine whether adjustments to the
   19          financial assurance are warranted and will adjust if necessary. Financial assurance can be
   20          provided in the form of a cash deposit, an irrevocable Letter of Credit (“LOC”) from a
   21          qualified bank, or by a guarantee from a qualified company. If the financial assurance is
   22          to be provided by a guarantor, the guarantor must have a credit rating of A3 (Moody’s) /
   23          A- (S&P) and show cash or cash equivalents equal to ten times the total value of the
   24          performance assurance on its most recently audited balance sheet.
   25
   26   Q.     How does the amount of collateral required by the XLPL Tariff compare to industry
   27          standards?
   28   A.     The Tariff requires more collateral than do most comparable tariffs of which I am aware.
   29          As I discuss below, collateral requirements are frequently calculated on the basis of
   30          minimum contract billing requirements multiplied by some period of time. Most calculate
   31          the requirement on the basis of a much shorter period than five years.

        Direct Testimony of Matthew DeCourcey                                       Page 13 of 29
        Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 4 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 14 OF 30




    1   Q.     In the context of stranded cost risk, why does the form of the financial security
    2          matter?
    3   A.     The most important consideration is whether a customer can secure its agreement for
    4          service using a guarantor or whether it must provide cash or an LOC as collateral. All else

   18          shared system costs, the burden on existing customers for those shared costs is reduced.
   19          This is why, all else equal, growth in utility sales tends to decrease rates.
   20
   21   Q.     Can you explain how that dynamic applies to adding XLPL customers?
   22   A.     OG&E’s rate structure, which includes required CIAC payments, rate riders, and base
   23          rates, requires large load customers to pay for the costs incurred by the Company for the
   24          specific purpose of providing them service, and also contribute to shared system costs. The
   25          result is that subsidization of the costs that are directly attributable to the new customer by
   26          other classes is avoided while the amount of revenue that must be collected from those
   27          other classes for shared system costs is reduced. The result is lower rates for OG&E’s
   28          existing customers.
